items.title: Employment law basics
items.source: Draft for review. Written by an AI assistant from general UK small-business knowledge, not from a cited document. Check every fact against current GOV.UK and regulator guidance, and have someone who does this work review it, before it is activated. Rules differ by country and change.
items.body: Employment law sets minimum rights that you cannot contract out of. Know whether someone is an employee, a worker or self-employed, because their rights differ. Employees and workers are entitled to at least the minimum wage, paid holiday, rest breaks and limits on weekly working time (in the UK, an average of 48 hours unless they opt out). Everyone is protected from discrimination on protected characteristics such as age, sex, race and disability, and employers must make reasonable adjustments for disabled staff. You must check the right to work before someone starts, and give a written statement of terms. Rules and qualifying periods change, so check current guidance.

questions.prompt: Which is a minimum right workers have?

options.text: Paid holiday and at least the minimum wage

questions.prompt: Why does it matter whether someone is an employee, a worker or self-employed?

options.text: Their legal rights, tax and insurance differ
It affects only the job title
It affects only the colour of the contract

questions.prompt: An employer must check this before someone starts work:

options.text: Nothing, because it is their problem

items.title: Patents and copyright
items.source: Draft for review. Written by an AI assistant from general UK small-business knowledge, not from a cited document. Check every fact against current GOV.UK and regulator guidance, and have someone who does this work review it, before it is activated. Rules differ by country and change.
items.body: Intellectual property is what your ideas create. Copyright protects original writing, images, music, software and designs automatically when they are created; in the UK no registration is needed. The creator is normally the first owner, but work an employee makes in the course of their job usually belongs to the employer, and work made by a contractor belongs to the contractor unless the rights are assigned in writing. A patent protects a new invention and must be applied for; the idea must be kept secret until you file. A trademark protects a brand name or logo for particular goods or services. Patents and trademarks need specialist advice.

options.text: Automatically, when original work is created

questions.prompt: Who normally owns work an employee creates in the course of their job?

What must you do to protect an invention with a patent?

options.text: Apply for it, and keep the idea secret until you file

items.title: Product safety and labels
items.source: Draft for review. Written by an AI assistant from general UK small-business knowledge, not from a cited document. Check every fact against current GOV.UK and regulator guidance, and have someone who does this work review it, before it is activated. Rules differ by country and change.
items.body: If you make or sell goods, you must sell safe products. Check what rules cover your product: some, such as toys, electrical items and cosmetics, need testing and a mark (in the UK, UKCA, and in some cases CE). Labels must carry the information the law requires, which can include the business name and address, usage instructions and warnings, quantity, batch number, and for food the ingredients with allergens highlighted. Keep test results and supplier records. If you learn a product is unsafe, stop selling it and tell customers and the authorities as required, and have a recall plan. Importers and sellers share responsibility with makers.

questions.prompt: Who is responsible for the safety of a product you sell?

options.text: You, as well as the maker
Nobody if it has a nice box

questions.prompt: Which is commonly required on a food label?
What should you do if you learn a product is unsafe?

options.text: Stop selling it and follow your recall plan

questions.prompt: Why keep test results and supplier records?

options.text: To prove the product meets the rules and to trace a problem

items.title: Registering for tax

items.body: Registering for tax tells the authorities you exist and which taxes you owe. A sole trader in the UK registers for self-assessment; a limited company is registered for corporation tax; an employer registers for PAYE; and VAT registration is required once taxable sales pass the threshold, and is optional below it. Register on time, because late registration can mean penalties. Keep the tax reference numbers safe and diarise the filing dates. Tax rules differ by country; ask an accountant which registrations apply to you and when.

options.text: To tell the tax authority which taxes you owe

items.title: Licences and permits
items.source: Draft for review. Written by an AI assistant from general UK small-business knowledge, not from a cited document. Check every fact against current GOV.UK and regulator guidance, and have someone who does this work review it, before it is activated. Rules differ by country and change.
items.body: Some activities need permission before you start: selling alcohol, serving hot food late at night, street trading, running a taxi, carrying waste, playing recorded music in public, and more. The rules and the issuing body, often the local authority or a sector regulator, depend on what you do and where. Trading without a required licence can be an offence, and an application can take weeks, so find out early, before you sign a lease or print a menu. Keep a list of each licence, its conditions and its renewal date, and display it if required.

options.text: Permission from an authority to carry out a regulated activity

questions.prompt: When should you find out which licences you need?

options.text: Before you commit to premises or open

questions.prompt: Who often issues licences for local trading activities?

options.text: Licences lapse, and trading without one can be an offence

items.title: Registering the business
items.source: Draft for review. Written by an AI assistant from general UK small-business knowledge, not from a cited document. Check every fact against current GOV.UK and regulator guidance, and have someone who does this work review it, before it is activated. Rules differ by country and change.
items.body: How you register depends on your structure. A sole trader trades in their own name and registers with the tax authority; a partnership registers its partners; a limited company is formed with the company registry and gets its own legal identity, with directors, shareholders, a registered office and a duty to file accounts and a confirmation statement each year. Check that the name is available and is not misleading, and keep the company's records and registers up to date. Registering is the start of ongoing duties, not a one-off. Ask an accountant or formation agent if you are not sure.

options.text: A separate legal entity from its owners

questions.prompt: Which does a limited company normally have to file each year?
Why check a business name before registering?

options.text: It must be available and not misleading
The registry chooses it for you

questions.prompt: Registering a company is:

options.text: A one-off task with no later duties

items.title: Legal duties when closing a business
items.source: Draft for review. Written by an AI assistant from general UK small-business knowledge, not from a cited document. Check every fact against current GOV.UK and regulator guidance, and have someone who does this work review it, before it is activated. Rules differ by country and change.
items.body: Closing a business properly protects you. Tell the tax authority and any registry; file final returns and accounts; pay what you owe; and keep records for the required period. If you employ people, give proper notice and follow the redundancy rules, which can include consulting staff and paying redundancy pay and wages owed. Cancel contracts, leases and licences in line with their terms, and tell customers and suppliers. Close or transfer data lawfully: delete personal data you no longer need and keep what the law requires. If you cannot pay your debts, take advice from a licensed insolvency practitioner before doing anything.

questions.prompt: Who must be told when a business closes?

options.text: The tax authority and the registry, as well as customers and staff

questions.prompt: What should happen to records when you close?

options.text: Keep them for the period the law requires

questions.prompt: What do you owe employees when you close the business?

options.text: Proper notice and pay, and redundancy rights where they apply

questions.prompt: You cannot pay your debts. What should you do first?

options.text: Take advice from a licensed insolvency practitioner
Take out new loans to pay the old ones
